Some tips for starters:

To me, in my financial position and my lifestyle it is:

Do not buy a car, Lease it.

People get down on this all the time but I assure you it is the best way to go, If you have decent credit, money in savings, and a steady income.

Find the absolute cheapest lease you can and get it.

Most people say "Why pay for something you don't own?"

Why? Because they depreciate, they are not "liquid" and they are a liability.

If you buy new or lease, you will lose the exact same amount of money over the first few years either way.

Do the math, take the car you have and add up every cent you have ever spent on it (except gas) subtract the (real) value of the car, then divide that number by the number of days you have had it.

A good lease get's you in around $7 a day. Where used cars usually come in around $10.

And the lease gets you free oil changes, free maintenance, and a complete warranty, and on top of that you get a free loaner if your car needs to be in the shop, you get free roadside assistance, the newer cars are safer, , , the list goes on and on.

Don't bother with financial advisors they will most likely try to put you into something called an investment-linked product. If you insist on getting a financial advisor, make sure they are fee-based not commission-based.

Don't leave money in a savings account as with most developed countries, the inflation rate is higher than the interest rate on those accounts meaning your savings depreciate over time instead of gaining value.

Best thing to do realistically if you have no idea what to do with your money. Choose an index fund and put your money in there.
Learn to cook, set up a food budget, plan dinner for a few days ahead and stick to it.
It's not income - expenses = savings. It's income - savings = expenses. Save a part of what you earn. The rest available is for spending.

Save money every paycheck. If you get a job with a decent 401k plan, get into it. Otherwise look at IRAs. Keep at it, week after week, year after year. One of these days if you're lucky, you'll be old. You don't want to be living in poverty when you're old.
When you finish school, keep living like you are in school for as long as it takes to pay off your debt.
Do you really need that thing? Or do you just want it? What is the trade-off? If you work a job that pays $15 an hour, is that lunch you are about to pay for worth a whole hour of you working?
Index funds are a lazy investors friend.

When it comes to investing, you're most likely going to be better off choosing a good mutual fund or index fund. Over the years, very few people are able to outperform the S&P 500, so you're safest bet is to invest in an S&P 500 index fund. Unless you have a crap ton of time to dedicate to researching individual stocks, it likely won't be worth it to invest in individual stocks.

The budget I use is relatively simple:

The 70/20/10 Rule:

When you recieve your paycheque, or any amount of cash from whatever your source of income may be, split it into three parts: EXPENSES(70%), SPENDING (Or 'short-term savings') (20%), and SAVINGS(10%).

*Feel free to adjust these percentages as required. The important thing here to do is to prioritize your spending habits and get somewhat organized.

The EXPENSES portion should cover most, if not all of your monthly expenses. (Bills, groceries, toiletries, ect) Whatever is left over should automatically be placed into your SAVINGS. Optionally, you may split it between SAVINGS and SPENDING. On the other hand, if not quite everything is covered by your EXPENSES, you may need to take money out from your reserved SPENDING budget to make up for the difference, and possibly re-adjust your percentages as required.

Another thing you can do in regards to spending from your SAVINGS account is to treat your savings as if it where a credit card or a bank. Put yourself into the mindset that you're not GIVING yourself money out of savings to spend, you are LOANING yourself your savings. Charge yourself interest whenever you spend money from your savings account. (I personally charge myself a flat rate of 5% interest for things that I deem to be "essential", and 10% or higher for more frivolous things.) This way, even if you break your budget, your savings will continue to grow with time. Albeit a little slower.
